languages.name: Indonesian
languages.reading:
Reading Indonesian:
- Pronouns signal register: gue/lo is casual, streetwise or young urban speech; aku/kamu is intimate or neutral; saya/Anda is formal.
- Discourse particles (sih, dong, deh, kok, kan, lho, ya, nih, tuh) carry tone, not content. Never translate them literally.
- Address terms (Pak, Bu, Mas, Mbak, Bang, Kak) show age and respect. Carry the relationship into the target language’s own forms of address.
- Subjects and tense are often left out. Infer them from context.
- Reduplication (anak-anak, pelan-pelan, tiba-tiba) means plurality, intensity or manner, never literal repetition.
- Foods, places and everyday items with no good equivalent (warung, angkot, ojek) keep their Indonesian names, without explanation.
languages.writing:
Writing Indonesian:
- Narration is standard, literary Indonesian (bahasa baku) that still flows naturally.
- Choose register per character: aku/kamu for peers and intimates, saya/Anda for formal speech, gue/lo only for casual young urban speech when the setting and voice suit it.
- Address elders and superiors with Bapak/Ibu or Pak/Bu, and use Mas/Mbak/Kak where natural.
- Use particles (sih, dong, kok, ya, kan) sparingly in dialogue to carry tone.
- Use di- passive where Indonesian prefers it, and repeat names instead of overusing dia/ia.
- Keep honorifics used with names (-san, -ssi, Khun) as they appear.
- Use “ ” for dialogue.

languages.name: English
languages.reading:
Reading English:
- English “you” carries no politeness level. Decide each relationship’s register (age, rank, closeness) from context and keep it consistent.
- Contractions, slang and clipped sentences mark casual speech; formal diction marks distance or rank.
- Replace idioms and wordplay with natural equivalents rather than literal translations.
- Transliterate names consistently (see the glossary).
languages.writing: Writing English: - Natural English novel prose. Dialogue in “ ”, nested quotes in ‘ ’. - Supply the subjects, articles and tense the source leaves out, inferring them from context. Narrate in past tense unless the book is in present tense. - Carry register through word choice, contractions and rhythm, not by sprinkling in slang words. - Keep honorific suffixes and titles used with names (-san, -ssi, Pak, Khun) as they appear, consistently. Kinship words used as pronouns become “I” and “you”. - Foods, places and cultural items with no good English equivalent stay romanized, in …, without explanation.

languages.name: Japanese
languages.reading:
Reading Japanese:
- Subjects are often left out. Infer them from context.
- Keigo levels, first-person pronouns and sentence endings (役割語) define each character’s voice and relationships. Carry them into the target language’s own register.
- Sentence-final particles (ね, よ, じゃん, だろ, かな) carry tone, not content.
- Honorific suffixes (-san, -kun, -chan, -sama, -senpai) show relationships. Keep them with names in Latin-script languages, or use the target language’s own forms of address.
- 擬音語 and 擬態語 become natural sound words or vivid verbs.
- 「」 marks dialogue; 『』 marks nested quotes or titles.
languages.writing:
Writing Japanese:
- Dialogue in 「」, thoughts or nested quotes in 『』 or （）. Use no Western quotation marks.
- Give each character consistent speech (役割語): first-person pronoun (俺, 僕, 私, あたし), sentence endings and politeness fit to age, personality and relationship.
- Set politeness by relationship: strangers, superiors and service settings use 敬語; friends and family use plain forms.
- Narration is plain past form, natural novel prose. Drop pronouns where Japanese would omit them; avoid overusing 彼/彼女.
- Write foreign names in katakana, consistently. Chinese names keep their kanji.
- Express sound and manner with 擬音語 and 擬態語 where natural.

languages.name: Korean
languages.names: Hangul for foreign names, following standard loanword spelling
languages.reading:
Reading Korean:
- Subjects are often left out. Infer them from context.
- Speech levels (반말, 해요체, 하십시오체) show age, rank and closeness. Carry them into the target language’s own register, consistently for each relationship.
- Kinship terms and titles (오빠, 언니, 형, 누나, 선배, 씨, 님) are used in place of names and “you”. Keep them with names in Latin-script languages where that reads naturally, or use the target language’s own forms of address.
- Sentence endings (-네, -지, -거든, -잖아) carry tone, not content.
- 의성어 and 의태어 become natural sound words or vivid verbs.
- Romanize names consistently (Revised Romanization unless the book shows another spelling).
languages.writing:
Writing Korean:
- Dialogue in “ ”, thoughts in ‘ ’, as Korean novels do.
- Set each pair of characters’ speech level by their relationship and keep it consistent: 반말 between close friends and to younger people, 해요체 for polite everyday speech, 하십시오체 in formal or official settings.
- Address people by name, title or kinship term (선배, 형, 오빠, 언니, 누나, 선생님, 씨, 님) rather than 너 or 당신 where Korean would.
- Narration is written style (-다 endings), usually past tense, natural novel prose. Drop pronouns where Korean omits them; avoid overusing 그/그녀.
- Write foreign names in Hangul following standard loanword spelling (외래어 표기법), consistently.
- Express sound and manner with 의성어 and 의태어 where natural.

languages.name: Chinese (Simplified)
languages.names: standard mainland Chinese transliterations for foreign names
languages.reading:
Reading Chinese:
- Chinese marks no tense. Infer time from context, aspect particles (了, 过, 着) and time words.
- Subjects and objects are often left out. Infer them from context.
- 您 versus 你, titles (老师, 师父, 先生) and kinship terms (哥, 姐, 叔, 阿姨) show respect and closeness. Carry them into the target language’s own register.
- Modal particles (吧, 呢, 啊, 嘛, 啦) carry tone, not content.
- 成语 and classical allusions become natural expressions with the same meaning, not literal glosses.
- Romanize names in Hanyu Pinyin for Latin-script languages, unless the book shows another spelling (Taiwan and Hong Kong names often have their own).
languages.writing:
Writing Simplified Chinese:
- Simplified characters with mainland vocabulary and conventions.
- Dialogue in “ ”, nested quotes in ‘ ’. Use full-width punctuation (，。！？：；、……——).
- Choose 您 or 你 by relationship. Carry tone in dialogue with modal particles (吧, 呢, 啊, 嘛, 呀) fitted to the speaker.
- Natural literary prose. Use 成语 where they fit, without overdoing them. Avoid overusing 他/她 and 的, and drop pronouns where Chinese would.
- Write foreign names with standard mainland transliterations, given name and surname joined by ·, consistently. Japanese and Korean names keep their Chinese characters where they have them.
- Express sound with natural Chinese onomatopoeia (拟声词).

languages.name: Chinese (Traditional)
languages.names: the transliterations usual in Taiwan for foreign names
languages.reading:
Reading Chinese:
- Chinese marks no tense. Infer time from context, aspect particles (了, 過, 着) and time words.
- Subjects and objects are often left out. Infer them from context.
- 您 versus 你, titles (老師, 師父, 先生) and kinship terms (哥, 姐, 叔, 阿姨) show respect and closeness. Carry them into the target language’s own register.
- Modal particles (吧, 呢, 啊, 嘛, 囉) carry tone, not content.
- 成語 and classical allusions become natural expressions with the same meaning, not literal glosses.
- Romanize names in Hanyu Pinyin for Latin-script languages, unless the book shows another spelling (Taiwan and Hong Kong names often have their own).
languages.writing:
Writing Traditional Chinese:
- Traditional characters with Taiwan vocabulary and conventions (計程車, 軟體, 影片, 網路).
- Dialogue in 「」, nested quotes in 『』. Use full-width punctuation (，。！？：；、……——).
- Choose 您 or 你 by relationship. Carry tone in dialogue with modal particles (吧, 呢, 啊, 嘛, 呀) fitted to the speaker.
- Natural literary prose. Use 成語 where they fit, without overdoing them. Avoid overusing 他/她 and 的, and drop pronouns where Chinese would.
- Write foreign names with the transliterations usual in Taiwan, given name and surname joined by ·, consistently. Japanese and Korean names keep their Chinese characters where they have them.
- Express sound with natural Chinese onomatopoeia (擬聲詞).

languages.name: Thai
languages.names: Thai script for foreign names, following Royal Institute transliteration
languages.reading:
Reading Thai:
- Thai has no spaces between words; spaces separate clauses and sentences.
- Tense is not marked. Infer it from context.
- Pronouns and kinship words used as pronouns (ผม, ฉัน, เรา, กู/มึง, พี่, น้อง) show gender, age, closeness and rudeness. Carry them into the target language’s own register.
- Particles (ครับ, ค่ะ, นะ, จ้ะ, สิ, เถอะ) carry politeness and tone, not content.
- Nicknames and the title คุณ before names are common. Keep each name and nickname consistent, romanized in the Royal Thai General System unless the book shows another spelling.
languages.writing:
Writing Thai:
- Thai script, with no spaces between words; a space separates clauses and sentences.
- Dialogue in “ ”.
- Choose pronouns per speaker and relationship and keep them consistent: ผม (men) or ฉัน/ดิฉัน (women) in polite speech, เรา or a nickname among friends, กู/มึง for rough speech, พี่/น้อง/ป้า/ลุง by age.
- Polite particles (ครับ for men, ค่ะ/คะ for women) and softeners (นะ, จ้ะ, สิ, เถอะ) carry politeness and tone; fit them to the speaker.
- Narration is natural written Thai novel prose. Drop pronouns where Thai would.
- Write foreign names in Thai script following Royal Institute transliteration, consistently.
- Render sound effects with Thai onomatopoeia.

languages.name: Vietnamese
languages.names: original spelling for Western names, Sino-Vietnamese readings for Chinese names
languages.reading:
Reading Vietnamese:
- Pronouns are kinship words (anh, chị, em, ông, bà, cô, chú, con, cháu) or pairs such as tôi–cậu and tao–mày. They show age, closeness and attitude: carry the relationship into the target language’s own register, not as literal kinship words, unless the target uses them the same way.
- Tense markers (đã, đang, sẽ) are optional. Infer time from context.
- Particles (ạ, nhé, nhỉ, à, hả, mà, chứ) carry politeness and tone, not content.
- Reduplicated words (từ láy) carry manner and intensity.
- Vietnamese names keep their diacritics in Latin-script languages.
languages.writing:
Writing Vietnamese:
- Full Vietnamese diacritics. Dialogue in “ ”.
- Choose a pronoun pair for each pair of characters by age, relationship and closeness, and keep it consistent: anh–em, chị–em, ông/bà–cháu, cô/chú–cháu, tớ–cậu between friends, tao–mày for rough speech, tôi with anh/chị/ông/bà in formal speech. Narration uses anh ấy, cô ấy, hắn or names, fitted to the narrator’s attitude.
- Particles (ạ, nhé, nhỉ, à, hả, mà, chứ) carry politeness and tone; fit them to the speaker.
- Natural modern prose. Use Sino-Vietnamese (Hán-Việt) words where they suit the register, not by default.
- Keep Western names in their original spelling; write Chinese names in their Sino-Vietnamese reading; romanize Japanese and Korean names. Keep all of them consistent.
- Express sound and manner with Vietnamese onomatopoeia and từ láy.
